What is actually feeling? What is actually feeling? [music fades] Thank you. You're on camera. It's like being next to a black person. Yeah, no — the other day I saw just Bobby's arm and I thought it was a black person.

Like, I'm pretty tan. I've never in my life seen a Japanese guy this dark. You're not in the sun. You're not like a day laborer. You're not out picking strawberries in the field.
So how do you get this dark? I don't know. What did your mom think when you popped out of her this dark? I bet you anything you were pale as a baby.

It's DVDASA with your hosts, David Choe and Asa Akira. We got special guest Critter Fleming. [shouting] Yeah, boy! I can never get through it clean. We got Val on the back end. Wait, you want to practice a little bit?

Me and Val went and got sushi. You have fucking white shit all over your mouth, and it's stuck between your teeth. What are you eating right now? You just ate something, it's all — no? White Cheetos, maybe? On the side of your mouth. Oh, you're right. It's looking disgusting. It's white shit. What were you eating right now?
We had sushi. Salmon, salmon sashimi, and a bowl. I got a bowl. And it's still all... all right. DC, come on back. So, Asa — we haven't seen Asa in a while.
She had a family emergency. Yeah, my grandma was dying, so I went to Japan. I said, hey Asa, you want to do a show this week? And she said, hey, my grandma's really sick.
I'm going to leave tomorrow. And we were like, okay. So she went to Japan to take care of a family emergency.

And immediately on Instagram, it's just a barrage of — like, you know, when I think of a family emergency, or someone in the family dying, I think black clothes, being at home a lot, and just being sad.
Well, first of all, it wasn't the funeral. My grandma's been super healthy her whole life, right? How old is she? The women in my family are so — it's scary how healthy we are.
How old is she? She's 93. Well, she died. Oh, she did? Yeah, a few days ago. But it's not sad. She died a few days ago? Yeah, but she was 93.

She lived an amazing life. It's not like she was young. Also, I'm sorry for your loss. Thank you. When did her husband die — like a million years ago, when he was 70-something? Yeah. He had a stroke and he was in a wheelchair my whole life.

So a huge part of your life was babysitting a dude. Yeah, that part sucks. But my grandpa was a diplomat, so she got to live all over the world. She's had three kids. And, by the way, Asians love having three kids.

I noticed this. Three sons, too. And threesomes. [beat] I don't know. So, no, it wasn't the funeral. My grandma got sick. We got a call she was diagnosed with cancer. She'd been on a cruise a week before that, totally healthy. What is the secret there?
What are they doing? Because actually, when I was in Japan and I got beat up and had to go to the prison hospital — well, it was a normal hospital, but I went in handcuffs.
And they found — the cop beat me up, but I also had kidney stones. I had no idea how you get kidney stones. I was like, what?

I don't drink or smoke. And he goes, you must adopt more Japanese diet. And the Japanese diet is fresh fish, vegetables, all that, but it's a lot of carbs. It was impossible for me to diet while I was in Japan.
So what are the Japanese people in your family doing to live to 93 and still be chilling on cruises? It's just the women, though. It's just the women.
I think the women are so overbearing that our men are just like, fuck it, I have to go. [laughing] So then what has she been doing?

So she has this really nice house, and she's just been fine. And then we got a call that she was diagnosed with cancer, and they were like, it's too late to operate or do anything — she might live through the weekend. So I booked a flight for the next day and flew out.

Hello — I'm talking about my girl dying. I mean, you look really good. I'd thank you, but be a little sensitive. I'm getting a little horny right now. Ew, can you stop? Let's talk about something else, then. No, I really — until you're not horny, I'm not. I'm not horny anymore. Okay, so...

So I went to see her at the hospital every morning. Of course Tony came with me — it was his first time in Japan. So we'd go see her in the morning, talk to her and stuff, and then for the rest of the day we were...
Talk to her, like, how? Well, no — she was already morphined up, so the most she could do was nod. She had tubes going down her throat.
Did she see you and go, oh? Yeah, she wasn't like [gasp] 'oh,' but I'd be like, hey, it's me, and she would nod. When was the last time you saw her?
Before I was in porn, like 10 years ago. Do you think she knows? No. Do you think that's why she goes? You should have told her. You think that's what happened? Are you crazy, Critter?

You don't understand. She'd be like, what's porn? You don't know that. She doesn't have internet. Trust me. You didn't want to be like, hey grandma. My mom told me that a few years ago my grandma asked her — she said, escorting is really popular in America, right?

And they were talking about me. So I think she did have a little bit of an intuition that I was doing something bad. [mock cheer] She's like, awesome. But porn's not bad. I'm very sick, I haven't seen you in 10 years, I want to know what you're doing.
Yeah. I didn't say anything. Do you have a backup line for when somebody asks and you don't want to tell them?

What do you say — in public, to strangers? Yeah, I just say I'm a housewife, because all conversation ends there. HH? Horny housewife? Horny housewife. But if you say any other job, people ask questions about it.
Just say you're a caregiver. Yeah, but even that I'd have to lie — like, I work with autistic kids or paralyzed people. Would you say the men in porn—
First of all, would you say the men in porn are abused victims? No. But one thing I noticed is they all have really strange relationships with their mothers.

Strange like what? Everyone's different, but some of them don't have moms, or grew up without a mom, or some are really close to their mom even at 50 — oddly close. And some of them hate their moms. But none of them have a totally normal relationship with their mom.

Well, everyone — every family, you have different relationships with all your — yeah, I guess. But I think it's true to a degree: the girls have daddy issues and the boys have mommy issues. You have no desire — you know, I've talked about it a little bit—

I don't do it to shock my parents, but basically my entire relationship with my family, my parents specifically, is built on lies, right? Let me give you an example. For Asian parents, mine were pretty supportive of my career, but they always had the 'yeah, but you should still go to college.'

And now that I've created this entire life for them and support them through art, they've taken a huge interest in art. They care about what I care about, because they're like, oh, this is how he makes money. So I go to the comic book store—
There are things that really upset my dad. I just did a song with Steve Lee and Money Mark called 'Gunk Boy' — oh no, it's the 'Hello' song. You don't like it?
I'll play it for you. We're just screaming in Korean. Oh, like random obscenities? It's just the shit we know how to say in Korean. It's like, thank you very much.

Are you hungry? Would you like to eat my fart? It's so delicious. That's literally it. And my mom and dad came up. I played them the 'Hallelujah' song. We recorded 12 songs, and I'm like, oh, I can't play that one, I can't play that one — there's literally like two songs I could play for them.

So they were in Big Bear for three days and I'm playing them the same two songs over and over. And they're like, hey, you've been here for three weeks and you only recorded two songs? I go, no, there's more songs. And then I'm like, [thinking] I'm not gonna play them—

—because I say 'fuck,' you know. And it's not like, hey mom and dad, I'm trying to shock you. Okay, I'm an adult, you're an adult — do you want to know the other things I did? They're like, yes. Okay, so I start playing—

—the song, and my mom is just laughing, my brother, my sister-in-law, they're laughing, and my dad's just doing the fake laugh — [mock] mm-hmm, mm-hmm. The song ends, we have dinner, and then later that night he's like, hey, come here—

—let me talk to you. And I'm like, [under breath] oh, here we go. And he goes, so what's up with that song? I go, what do you mean, I'm a fucking grown man. He's like, it's a little upsetting, you know, as your father it's a little upsetting to me. I go, why? Because you dishonored the—
Yeah, he's like, what if my friends hear it? It always comes down, for Asian parents, to 'what are my friends gonna think?'

What am I supposed to tell my friends you do? They're very concerned about that — which money usually solves. Like when I'm talking to Steve, hey, let's do this, let's do this, he's like, dude, my mom will kill me.

'My mom will kill me.' But I go, your brother whips his dick out on stage every night. And he goes, but he makes money doing it, so then it's okay, right? So I go, dad, you don't fucking get it, man — this song's gonna be huge. I was in Korea 10 years ago and I checked out the punk rock scene—

—and it was fucking horrible, wannabe Green Day shit. I'm like, this is the most punk rock song ever, dad. And he's like, I don't like it, it's a big disgrace to our family, to our country, to our culture. And I was like, yes! And I could have easily—

—not shared that song with him, but I did. Not that I want to piss him off to make me feel good — but it bothered him to the point where he didn't let it go. That was a few weeks ago, and every day I see him he's like, that song is not going to be—

—on the album, right? And I go, are you fucking kidding me, you're still talking about that? On the reverse end of the spectrum, my mom is like, play that song again — she's a born-again Christian, you know what I'm saying, 'you son of a bitch, eat my ass,' all this shit.

She's gone to the other end of the spectrum where she wants me to overshare with her. Well, you should start — no. Like, my dad's birthday is very close to Father's Day, so he never wants presents anymore. I got him a watch—

—that's more expensive than anything I ever got my mom, and I got it just because I know he'd never wear it — just to piss my mom off. And she's like, hmm. And he's like, yeah, I don't want that. And now your mom's just gonna expect—

—something even more expensive that I'm never gonna get her. And he's like, I just want to go see this movie. And I go, okay. My dad watches every movie that comes out in theaters. He saw Brokeback Mountain. Any movie that comes out, he'll go watch it.

So I go, okay cool — Transformers is out, the new Tom Cruise movie, The Raid 2, we can see any one of these. And he goes, I want to see this movie about two kids who have cancer who fall in love. Oh, it's a really good book. I go, this shit sounds horrible. And he goes—

—and then my brother calls me and goes, he hasn't stopped talking about wanting to see this movie with you. I go, can I just get him the ticket? He goes, no, he wants to watch it with you. Of course — it's his fucking birthday. And I go, oh fuck. So we go watch it, and everyone in the—

And everyone in the theater — it's a sob fest. I'm like, Jesus Christ. But before the movie we had 15 minutes, we got to the theater early, and there's a bookstore next door that sells comics and whatever. So I go, hey, I'm—

my parents like to eat at seven, they don't eat at nine, that's way too late. All the places that can seat us are like, we can see you at 10. And I'm like, hold on, give me a second. I go, dad, is this true? He's like, yeah, it's cool, what's the big deal? And the conveyor belt places in America were really shitty. Really shitty. Dollar sushi.

'It's rad. It's pretty cool.' I'll agree with that. I go, you're fucking rich, dude. I'm rich, so that means you're rich. Why don't you go to Nobu?

And I go, this is how you should eat with mom every night. It's your fucking birthday, and you took me to a Christian movie at the dollar theater in Pasadena with sticky floors and sticky seats.
Like, what the hell? Just live it up and then die. That's it, that's all that's left. So — I don't even know. Yeah, it was crazy, but it was weird being out.

I go, but you know that, A, it's illegal, and two, I'm asking you not to do it. He's like, I can't help it, I love reading your mail — all these people, they like you and stuff.
